scenarios.name: Bundle, no board, then a follow-up

card.problem: Explain what a Bundle is in Android and when to use it
card.heard: explain Bundle and when to use it
card.say: A Bundle is a container that holds data as key-value pairs. Android uses it to pass small amounts of data between screens and to save state. I'd use it for simple things like an ID, a title or a filter, not for large objects or images. When the system kills the app in the background, the Bundle is how the screen gets its state back.

results.detail: none
PASS: The SAY line plainly defines a Bundle as a key-value data container and explains its uses in spoken English, with no code.

card.problem: Explain what a Bundle is in Android and when to use it
card.constraints: ["Bundle must stay small; large data causes TransactionTooLargeException"]
card.heard: what happens if the Bundle gets too large
card.say: The system has a hard limit on saved state, about one megabyte. If I go over it, the app crashes with a TransactionTooLargeException. So I keep the Bundle small: an ID, a title, a filter. For a big object, I save the ID and reload the data from the database or the network. For a large image, I pass a file path or a URL, not the image itself.

results.detail: none
PASS: The SAY explains the ~1MB limit and TransactionTooLargeException, directly answering what happens when a Bundle is too large.

transcript: Interviewer: Can you explain what a Bundle is in Android and when you would use it?
Interviewer: What happens if the Bundle gets too large?

scenarios.name: Design, then code, then principle

card.problem: Design a ChatGPT-style chat screen on Android
card.heard: design a ChatGPT-style chat screen on Android
card.say: I'd start with the message list as the base. Each message is one item in a LazyColumn, keyed by its id, so new messages don't rebuild the whole list. The input box sits at the bottom, and the send button stays disabled while a reply is still streaming in.

results.detail: none
PASS: SAY opens a step-by-step design by scoping the main parts (message list as base, LazyColumn keyed by id, input box, send button state) without writing code or a full essay.

card.problem: Design a ChatGPT-style chat screen on Android
card.heard: write the ViewModel that holds the message list
card.say: I'll keep the list in a StateFlow of an immutable list. The UI collects it as state, so each change gives a new list and Compose redraws only what changed. I'll add a send function that appends the user message first, then a placeholder for the reply. The reply text updates that same item as chunks arrive.
card.type: add@ChatViewModel: data class Message(val id: String, val role: Role, val text: String, val streaming: Boolean = false) ⏎  ⏎ class ChatViewModel : ViewModel() { ⏎     private val _messages = MutableStateFlow<List<Message>>(emptyList()) ⏎     val messages: StateFlow<List<Message>> = _messages.asStateFlow() ⏎  ⏎     fun send(input: String) { ⏎         val userMsg = Message(id = UUID.randomUUID().toString(), role = Role.USER, text = input) ⏎         val replyId = UUID.randomUUID().toString() ⏎         val reply = Message(id = replyId, role = Role.ASSISTANT, text = "", streaming = true) ⏎         _messages.update { it + userMsg + reply } ⏎     } ⏎  ⏎     fun onChunk(replyId: String, chunk: String) { ⏎         _messages.update { list -> ⏎             list.map { if (it.id == replyId) it.copy(text = it.text + chunk) else it } ⏎         } ⏎     } ⏎  ⏎     fun onDone(replyId: String) { ⏎         _messages.update { list -> ⏎             list.map { if (it.id == replyId) it.copy(streaming = false) else it } ⏎         } ⏎     } ⏎ }

results.detail: add@ChatViewModel: data class Message(val id: String, val role: Role, val text: String, val streaming: Boolean = false)

PASS: The SAY section provides a concise spoken lead-in explaining the StateFlow/immutable list approach, and TYPE contains a compact Kotlin ViewModel snippet with Message data class, StateFlow, and send/onChunk/onDone functions.

card.problem: Design a ChatGPT-style chat screen on Android
card.heard: why StateFlow over LiveData
card.say: There are two reasons. First, StateFlow is a plain Kotlin flow, so it works the same in the ViewModel and in Compose. Second, it always has a current value, so a new screen gets the latest list right away. LiveData is tied to the Android lifecycle, and it's harder to combine with other flows. For a stream that updates many times a second, StateFlow is the simpler fit.

results.detail: PASS: The SAY clearly explains the choice of StateFlow over LiveData (plain Kotlin flow, always has a current value, easier flow combination, lifecycle coupling of LiveData) in the context of the chat screen's message list.

transcript: Interviewer: How would you design a chat screen like ChatGPT on Android?
Interviewer: Okay, can you write the ViewModel that holds the message list?
Interviewer: Why did you pick StateFlow over LiveData there?

scenarios.name: Switch A to B while the board still shows A

card.problem: Implement load() in the ViewModel using RxJava
card.heard: switch from RxJava to Kotlin Flow
card.say: Okay, I'll switch this part to Flow. I'll keep the same loading, data and error states. The repository call becomes a Flow, and I'll collect it in viewModelScope. I'll also use stateIn so the UI gets a StateFlow, and the collection stops when the ViewModel is cleared.
card.type: replace@ChatViewModel: class ChatViewModel(private val repo: ChatRepository) : ViewModel() { ⏎     sealed class State { ⏎         object Loading : State() ⏎         data class Data(val messages: List<Message>) : State() ⏎         data class Error(val message: String) : State() ⏎     } ⏎  ⏎     private val _state = MutableStateFlow<State>(State.Loading) ⏎     val state: StateFlow<State> = _state ⏎  ⏎     fun load() { ⏎         viewModelScope.launch { ⏎             _state.value = State.Loading ⏎             repo.messages() ⏎                 .catch { e -> _state.value = State.Error(e.message ?: "Unknown error") } ⏎                 .collect { list -> _state.value = State.Data(list) } ⏎         } ⏎     } ⏎ }

results.detail: Kotlin Flow instead of RxJava
PASS: SAY frames the switch as a plan ("I'll switch this part to Flow"), doesn't claim completion, and the TYPE migrates load() to Flow with no RxJava remaining.

transcript: Interviewer: Please implement load() in the ViewModel. You can use RxJava.

[board] class ChatViewModel(private val repo: ChatRepository) : ViewModel() { |     private val disposables = CompositeDisposable() |     fun load() { |         disposables.add(repo.messages().subscribeOn(Schedulers.io()).subscribe { messages.postValue(it) }) |     } | }
Interviewer: I'd rather not use RxJava here. Let's switch this to Kotlin Flow.

scenarios.name: Scrolling is not a change

card.problem: Walk through the feed API: GET /v1/feed with cursor and limit, returning posts and pagination metadata
card.heard: Walk me through this API
card.say: This is the feed endpoint. The app sends a cursor and a limit, and gets back a page of posts. Each post has an ID, a time, the content and the author. The author has an ID, a name and an avatar URL. The pagination metadata tells the app where it is. "After" and "before" are the cursors for the next and previous page, and "reachedEnd" says there's nothing more.

scenarios.name: Follow-up inside a follow-up, then back

card.problem: Design the data layer for an offline-first news feed
card.heard: Who owns the cache?
card.say: The repository owns it. The data source just reads and writes rows. It doesn't decide when to refresh or when to drop old items. That rule lives in the repository, so the screen never touches the cache directly.

results.detail: PASS: The SAY explicitly states the repository owns the cache and clarifies the data source only reads/writes rows, directly answering the ownership question.

card.problem: Design the data layer for an offline-first news feed
card.heard: Please continue with the data layer
card.say: Okay, so the layers are: the screen, the repository, and two data sources, one for the network and one for the local database. The repository is the only one that decides where data comes from. When the screen asks for the feed, the repository returns the cached list first, so the user sees something right away. Then it fetches fresh data from the network and saves it to the database. The screen just collects a Flow, so it updates by itself when new data arrives.

results.detail: PASS: The SAY resumes the layered data design (screen, repository, network/local sources) and describes cache-first behavior without re-justifying the repository's existence.

transcript: Interviewer: Design the data layer for an offline-first news feed.
Interviewer: Wait, why a repository at all?
Interviewer: And who owns the cache, the repository or the data source?
Interviewer: Okay, makes sense. Please continue with the data layer.

scenarios.name: Switch problems and return

card.problem: Compare Service and WorkManager
card.heard: What is the difference between a Service and a WorkManager job?
card.say: A Service runs code in the background, but it doesn't survive a reboot, and the system can kill it. WorkManager is for work that must finish, even after a restart. It saves the job, adds constraints like network or charging, and retries with backoff. So for a one-off upload I'd use WorkManager, and for something tied to the app running, like music, a Service.

results.detail: PASS: The SAY correctly distinguishes Service (background execution, not reboot-persistent, killable) from WorkManager (guaranteed completion, persistence across restart, constraints, retry/backoff) and gives appropriate use cases.

card.problem: Design an image loading library for Android
card.heard: Now let's go back to the image loading library
card.say: Okay, back to the image loading library. Before I design it, I'd like to agree on the main goal: images should show up fast and never block the UI. Then I'd split it into a few parts. A request goes into a queue, a memory cache is checked first, then the disk cache, then the network. I'd start with the request flow and the memory cache, because that's the core.
card.then: Wait for the interviewer to pick the first part.

results.detail: PASS: The SAY explicitly returns to the image loading library, states a goal, and begins outlining the design (request queue, memory/disk cache, network).

scenarios.name: An early constraint survives a long discussion

card.problem: Design a notes app that works fully offline (hard requirement)
card.heard: What would you build next?
card.say: Next I'd build the local data layer, because offline is the hard requirement. I'd start with a Room database for notes, and a repository that reads and writes only to it. The UI would observe the database through Flow, so the screen always shows saved data, even with no network. After that, I'd add a small sync layer that queues local changes and sends them when a connection comes back.

results.detail: ["Must work fully offline, hard requirement"]
PASS: The card's next step is a local Room database and repository with Flow-observed UI, directly honoring the offline hard requirement, plus a queued sync layer that doesn't contradict it.
